item.title: Capital no longer creates jobs, and AI is compounding the issue: Yatish Rajawat of Hundred Million Jobs
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, K Yatish Rajawat of Hundred Million Jobs said MSMEs, data laws, entrepreneurship and reskilling will shape the next wave of employment in the country.
item.content:encoded:
India's growth model is quietly severing the link between investment and employment, said K Yatish Rajawat, Co-founder of Hundred Million Jobs, a non-profit initiative to create 100 million net jobs in India over the next decade.

Capital is no longer creating jobs at scale, he said, at TechSparks, YourStory's flagship tech-startup summit.

The employment problem is different across cities, be it Delhi, Mumbai or Bengaluru, he observed. In Bengaluru, for instance, the debate is often around AI and its impact on jobs.

The damage began roughly a decade ago on the factory floors, driven by automation, he opined. Even a firm with a turnover of Rs 10 crore or Rs 50 crore now has robots, he said, and the machines are constantly evolving and getting better. They no longer simply move a widget from one point to another. They respond to their surroundings, and handle a range of materials, including cloth and paper, not just sheet metal, said Rajawat.

Even labour-intensive work such as welding and forging has been impacted due to automation, he said. He expects services to follow suit.

Referring to a book by Nobel Prize winners and MIT professors, Daron Acemoglu and Simon Johnson, Power and Progress: Our Thousand-Year Struggle Over Technology and Prosperity, Rajawat said while technology eventually adds jobs, it does so with a lag.

The people who lose work, he argued, are rarely the ones who gain from the new roles being created. While someone in their twenties may adapt to the shift, an employee in their forties or fifties is unlikely to do so, he added.

Trends reshaping the economy

Rajawat identified three trends reshaping the economy.

The old formula, wherein Rs 100 crore of investment generates around 10,000 jobs, no longer holds, he said. Plants manufacturing mobile phone and electric vehicles are heavily automated, and schemes such as the production-linked incentive are tied to capital rather than employment.

The second trend is the impact of AI and automation. AI is already affecting white-collar work across sectors. MSMEs, which he called the country's largest job engine, are also losing jobs to automation.

The third, which, he said, gets too little attention, is platform consolidation.

Rajawat argued that dominant ecommerce and social media platforms hold consumer data, which new entrepreneurs need, and this kind of monopoly prevents new businesses from succeeding. If entrepreneurship stalls, so does job creation, he said.

What Hundred Million Jobs is doing

Hundred Million Jobs works on ground projects, research, and advocacy across the country.

A consortium of six companies is helping the Rajasthan government turn its skilling mission into a jobs mission, on the premise that skilling is an input and jobs are the output that matters. In Kolhapur, the non-profit body is working with foundry and die-casting units to cut energy costs by shifting to renewables so that firms can compete, export and hire.

On the legal front, Hundred Million Jobs has formed a working group with sitting and former high court and Supreme Court judges. It is also planning a pilot with a high court to clear case backlog in a particular district using technology. Rajawat said slow enforcement of contracts and patents leaves solo entrepreneurs defenceless against large clients who do not pay.

The initiative is also lobbying for changes to data-ownership laws and for MSMEs to receive the same recognition as tech startups in entrepreneurship awards.

Rajawat also said Hundred Million Jobs has urged the skilling ministry to recognise displaced workers as a category needing support. And he wants the market, not the state, to provide support.

"Some of you should set up a company which does reskilling of displaced workers," he told the audience, calling it both a business opportunity and a way to create jobs.

A special thank you to Rawbare, our gifting partner, for adding a thoughtful touch to the TechSparks 2026 experience and making this year's edition even more memorable.

item.title: Talent diplomacy may become the next driver of global economic growth
item.description: As ageing populations and skill shortages weigh on economies worldwide, countries are looking beyond immigration to build structured talent partnerships. India has an opportunity to emerge as a trusted global hub for workforce readiness, backed by skills training, tech and verifiable credentials.
item.content:encoded:
The drivers of economic power have always traditionally been accessing to capital, energy, technology, and markets; but more nations are now running up against that much more difficult resource to generate fast talent.

Unlike capital, talent is not something that can be conjured out of thin air overnight, it takes years to educate, train, and ready the workforce. But at the same time that world economies are in need of more workers, the number of people available is declining.

Healthcare offers one of the most transparent indicators of this situation. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates a shortfall of 11. 1 million health and care professionals worldwide by 2030. Other sectors including manufacturing logistics hospitality, construction, and trades are experiencing similar pressures. Workforce numbers in many advanced countries are declining even as the need for core functions increases. There are declining numbers of people undertaking physically demanding jobs, leaving serious structural deficits difficult to address solely through large-scale migration.

What's left unsaid is huge: skills shortages are no longer an employment issue. They are a drag on economic growth. Countries are free to scale up investments in infrastructure, industrial capacity and technological advances, if they lack the people to run them, where is the growth?

Talent partnerships reshape economic diplomacy

Demographic decline is prompting governments to reconsider avenues for future growth. One-third of the EU population will be over 65 by the year 2050 and countries, including Japan and Germany, are already experiencing dire skill shortages within care and the healthcare sector.

Their answer has gone further than simply immigration reform. Germany's Skilled Immigration Act, Japan's increases of avenues for foreign workers and the EU's Talent Partnerships are part of a bigger change: policy makers are now starting to see "talent as a strategic asset".

These agreements are increasingly targeted on preparing the work force, recognising qualifications and moving workers, not only on visas. As countries used to compete for market access, energy, and supply chains, they are now forming partnerships to enjoy access to skilled people.

That may be one of the biggest changes to economic diplomacy in the coming decade.

India can become a global hub for workforce readiness

India’s opportunity should not be framed as the export of labour. It lies in becoming a trusted global centre for workforce readiness.

India’s domestic healthcare requirements must remain central to this approach. Responsible mobility should generate additional training capacity rather than draw indiscriminately from areas that already.

Encouragingly, this shift is already visible in policy. India plans to establish 30 Skill India International Centres focused on preparing individuals for overseas employment, while NSDC has certified over 22,455 candidates for international mobility over the past three years. The 2026 International Mobility Framework released by NITI Aayog further signals a shift in thinking, calling for greater state participation in global workforce mobility. Collectively, this suggests a larger shift where mobility of the workforce is a national asset helping create stronger economic partnerships, talent corridors, and help make India a trusted partner for the global workforce.

Technology must build trusted talent corridors

As opposed to taking over the role of educators, AI technology can assist in individualised learning, language training, workplace simulations, and competency evaluation.

Technology may minimise the information discrepancies, which have traditionally plagued international recruiting efforts. Employers require assurance that the credentials and experience are legitimate, while applicants require assurance about the legitimacy of the offer itself, along with its costs and conditions of employment.

This is increasingly becoming a competitive differentiator. ASEAN chases digital recognition of qualifications and credentials to enable smoother cross-border mobility.

For India, the opportunity is to make workforce readiness portable, verifiable and trusted. Technology can become the infrastructure that allows Indian professionals to prove their preparedness across markets, reducing friction for both employers and destination countries.

Though India's demographic weight is not the only one in an increasingly crowded field of developing countries, that invested years in creating structured talent corridors with host countries. Globally, over 8,000 nurses from Germany's Triple Win programme through government to government-built recruitment and training setups, while Japan's long standing health mobility corridors with Indonesia, the Philippines and Vietnam span language training, credentialing, and governance.

The real competition, therefore, is not for vacancies. It is for trust. Workforce shortages as a strategic challenge for ageing economies creates diplomacy where workforce readiness determines which nations become indispensable partners in supporting global growth.

(Mayank Kumar is the Co-founder & CEO of BorderPlus)

item.title: Lessons in Chemistry: 5 Takeaways from Bonnie Garmus’ Novel
item.description: Discover five powerful lessons from Lessons in Chemistry by Bonnie Garmus about equality, ambition, independent thinking, and self-worth.
item.content:encoded:
Lessons in Chemistry by Bonnie Garmus is a thought-provoking novel about ambition, gender inequality, motherhood, and the courage to challenge social expectations.

Set in the 1960s, the story follows Elizabeth Zott, a brilliant chemist whose professional ambitions are constantly challenged by a society that believes women belong in the kitchen rather than the laboratory.

When Elizabeth unexpectedly becomes the host of a cooking television show, she uses the opportunity to teach more than recipes. Through science, she encourages women to think independently, question established beliefs, and recognise their own abilities.

The novel offers several meaningful lessons about self-worth, equality, and the importance of refusing to let society define who we can become.

5 Powerful ideas in Lessons in Chemistry by Bonnie Garmus

1. Never let society define your potential

One of the most important lessons in Lessons in Chemistry is that your potential should never be determined by society's expectations.

Elizabeth Zott is an exceptionally talented scientist, but she faces discrimination because she is a woman working in a male-dominated field. Instead of being judged solely on her knowledge and abilities, she repeatedly encounters people who underestimate her because of her gender.

Her experiences highlight how social stereotypes can prevent talented individuals from reaching their full potential. Elizabeth refuses to accept these limitations as the truth about herself. She continues pursuing her interests and challenges the assumptions that attempt to hold her back.

The lesson is simple: your abilities are not limited by what others believe you can achieve. Whether in your career, education, or personal life, you deserve the opportunity to explore your potential without being restricted by outdated expectations.

2. Question everything instead of accepting it blindly

Elizabeth approaches life with the curiosity of a scientist. She believes in examining evidence, asking questions, and understanding why things happen rather than accepting conventional wisdom without thinking.

This mindset becomes particularly important when she begins hosting her cooking show, Supper at Six. Although the programme is designed around cooking, Elizabeth introduces scientific explanations and encourages her audience to understand the processes behind everyday tasks.

Her approach transforms an ordinary television show into an opportunity for women to learn, think critically, and develop confidence in their own intelligence.

The novel reminds readers that questioning established ideas is not necessarily an act of rebellion. Sometimes, it is the first step towards progress.

In everyday life, this means examining the beliefs we inherit, questioning unfair traditions, and making decisions based on reason rather than fear of judgement. Independent thinking allows us to recognise when something needs to change.

3. Women deserve equal opportunities and respect

Gender inequality is a central theme throughout Lessons in Chemistry. Elizabeth encounters professional discrimination, unequal treatment, and assumptions about what women should do with their lives.

Her experiences reflect a broader social problem: women's achievements have often been overlooked simply because they do not fit traditional expectations.

Through Elizabeth's journey, Bonnie Garmus illustrates how exhausting it can be to prove one's competence in an environment where others are unwilling to offer equal opportunities. Elizabeth must work harder to have her knowledge recognised, even when her qualifications speak for themselves.

However, the novel also demonstrates the importance of women supporting one another and recognising their shared potential.

The lesson extends beyond the workplace. Equality means respecting women's choices, valuing their contributions, and allowing them to pursue careers and ambitions without being forced into predefined roles.

A person's capabilities should determine their opportunities, not their gender.

7 Things to Accept About Yourself Before You Turn 30

4. Intelligence and confidence can change the way people think

Elizabeth's transformation into a television personality demonstrates that knowledge can be a powerful tool for challenging social attitudes.

Rather than abandoning her scientific background to fit the expectations of a cooking show, she brings science into the kitchen. She explains cooking through chemistry and treats her viewers as intelligent individuals capable of understanding complex ideas.

Her approach challenges the assumption that domestic responsibilities and intellectual pursuits must exist separately. It also gives women a platform to engage with science in a way that traditional institutions have often denied them.

Elizabeth's confidence is not about proving that she is better than everyone else. It comes from knowing the value of her knowledge and refusing to make herself smaller to satisfy other people's expectations.

This lesson encourages readers to embrace their expertise, communicate their ideas clearly, and trust their ability to make a difference.

Sometimes, changing people's perspectives begins with one person who is willing to challenge the familiar and present a different way of thinking.

5. Family and personal identity can exist beyond traditional roles

Another meaningful lesson from Lessons in Chemistry is that people should be allowed to define family and identity on their own terms.

Elizabeth's life challenges conventional ideas about motherhood, relationships, and women's responsibilities. Her experiences show that being a mother does not mean abandoning one's ambitions, just as pursuing a career does not make someone less capable of caring for a family.

The novel explores how people navigate grief, parenthood, relationships, and the expectations placed upon them. It presents a more nuanced understanding of what it means to build a fulfilling life.

Elizabeth refuses to accept that she must choose between being intellectually ambitious and being a devoted parent. Instead, she creates a life that reflects her circumstances, values, and priorities.

For readers, the lesson is that there is no single formula for a meaningful life. People have different ambitions, responsibilities, and definitions of happiness.

Rather than measuring ourselves against conventional milestones, we can focus on building lives that align with our own values and allow us to grow.

Final thoughts

Lessons in Chemistry by Bonnie Garmus is more than a novel about a scientist navigating a world that underestimates her. It is a story about challenging inequality, embracing curiosity, and refusing to let other people's assumptions determine your future.

Through Elizabeth Zott's experiences, readers are reminded that intelligence deserves recognition, women deserve equal opportunities, and personal ambition should not be sacrificed to satisfy society's expectations.

The five lessons from the book encourage us to question outdated beliefs, trust our abilities, and create lives that reflect who we truly are. Whether you are navigating your career, questioning social norms, or discovering your own identity, Elizabeth's journey offers a powerful reminder that you do not have to fit into someone else's definition of success.

Ultimately, Lessons in Chemistry encourages readers to approach life with curiosity, courage, and the confidence to challenge what they have been told is possible.

item.title: Workshaala targets Rs 1,000 Cr revenue as it scales enterprise workspace business
item.description:
Workshaala targets Rs 1,000 Cr revenue as it scales enterprise workspace business
India's offices are being reinvented, and Workshaala wants to be the company that runs them. The enterprise workspace provider has set out a Rs 1,000 crore revenue vision for its next phase of growth, built on a fo
item.content:encoded:
India's offices are being reinvented, and Workshaala wants to be the company that runs them. The enterprise workspace provider has set out a Rs 1,000 crore revenue vision for its next phase of growth, built on a footprint that already spans 3.5 million sq ft of serviceable area: 75,000 seats across 25 centres in 10 Indian cities.

The announcement follows a landmark moment for the company. Workshaala recently delivered what it describes as the world's largest service-platform workplace transaction, a deal that is now live within its existing footprint.

For the company's leadership, that transaction is less a finish line than a proof point. It shows the model works at the very top end of enterprise demand, and that it is ready to be replicated across the country.

From proof point to growth platform

Workshaala is clear that the Rs 1,000 crore target is not a fundraising story or a projection built on potential. It is a revenue roadmap anchored in a model the company has already tested at the largest scale in its category.

The timing reflects a market at an inflection point. India's technology and services economy is expected to add millions of white-collar seats over the next decade. Grade-A workspace demand is outpacing supply in every major city. And enterprises are taking a hard look at the economics of traditional real estate, seeking flexibility, cost predictability and operational efficiency without the weight of long-term leases.

That is precisely the gap Workshaala was built to fill. With execution already proven, the company sees scaling not as an option, but as the logical next step.

Four pillars to Rs 1,000 crore

Rather than a single bet on one city or one client segment, Workshaala's growth plan rests on four pillars, each already in motion.

1. Pan-India expansion. The company is growing across Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai and Mumbai, with emerging Tier II hubs such as Indore, Coimbatore and Chandigarh close behind. Enterprises increasingly want a single partner that can deliver consistent workspace standards in every city they operate in. Workshaala's playbook is designed to travel.

2. A technology layer beneath the real estate. Workshaala runs a platform that manages occupancy, utilization, service delivery and facility operations in real time. This lets it operate 75,000 seats across 25 centres with the discipline of a technology business rather than the margins of a facilities operator, and allows revenue to scale faster than headcount.

3. Enterprise-grade service delivery. Large corporates do not switch workspace partners lightly. They need assurance on uptime, compliance, safety, and consistency at scale. Workshaala's landmark transaction gives prospective clients a live reference they can visit before they sign, rather than a promise in a pitch deck.

4. Strategic ecosystem partnerships. Instead of competing with developers, landlords and corporate real estate teams, Workshaala works alongside them. It positions itself as the operating layer that makes large commercial assets enterprise-ready, a model that compounds as more partners plug into the platform.

Taken together, the pillars describe a company that is not chasing growth for its own sake, but extending a model it has already validated at scale.

Built for the GCC wave

No discussion of enterprise workspace demand in India is complete without Global Capability Centers, and this is where Workshaala sees its sharpest fit.

GCCs come with distinct expectations. Parent companies mandate strict security and compliance standards. Headcount plans can double within a year. And the space has to feel world-class from day one.

Workshaala's answer is to pair real estate execution with its live occupancy and service-delivery platform. Instead of waiting months for a customized build-out, a GCC can move into managed, technology-enabled space that is enterprise-ready from the outset. It can then grow from 200 seats to 2,000 without renegotiating its entire real estate strategy.

Standardized service levels across 25 centres in 10 cities mean every GCC location runs on the same playbook, with the uptime guarantees, compliance rigor, and reporting discipline a global headquarters expects.

As India cements its role as the world's hub for innovation and operations, GCCs are emerging as one of the fastest-growing segments of Workshaala's enterprise pipeline.

The road ahead

The next decade will decide how enterprise India works, and where. Companies want space that scales with them, runs reliably in every city and frees capital from long leases.

Workshaala is betting that the winners in this market will be operators who combine physical execution with a technology backbone, and that a model proven at the largest scale can be repeated city by city.

The Rs 1,000 crore milestone is the company's way of measuring that bet. With 75,000 seats already live, a reference transaction enterprises can walk into, and a growing GCC pipeline, Workshaala is entering its growth decade from a position of proof rather than promise.

item.title: Matiks raises $10M in pre-Series A round led by General Catalyst
item.description: The company said it will use the funding to expand internationally, develop new games and social experiences, and launch an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered game creation platform that will enable users to build and publish games without writing code.
item.content:encoded:
Bengaluru-based social gaming platform Matiks has raised $10 million in a pre-Series A funding round led by General Catalyst. The round also saw participation from entrepreneur Ronnie Screwvala and existing investors Info Edge Ventures, Tanglin Venture Partners, and Untitled Ventures.

According to a statement by the company, the fresh capital will be used to expand internationally, develop new games and social experiences, and launch an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered game creation platform that will enable users to build and publish games without writing code.

Founded in 2024, Matiks develops games centred on mathematics, memory, logic and puzzles, combining competitive gameplay with social features.

In September 2026, 2.2 million people played 48 million games on the platform. Its daily active users have more than doubled since June to over 300,000, with early engagement emerging in markets including Japan, the US and South Korea, the compamy said.

“Over the last decade, we have made it incredibly easy to consume content but have done far less to make using our brains equally entertaining. We started Matiks with a simple belief: using your brain can be just as fun and addictive as any other form of entertainment," said Sudhanshu Bhatia, co-founder and chief executive officer of Matiks.

"Our ambition is to make mind sports as culturally relevant as physical sports and esports - giving mental athletes, puzzlers, and competitive players the visibility, communities, and recognition they deserve. With AI, we want anyone, anywhere in the world, to create a brain game that millions can play. We are not trying to get people off their phones; we are trying to give them something better to do on them,” he added.

The company said users who complete a seven-day streak show 62% retention one month later, while some early cohorts have retained 32% of users at week 52. Its recently launched single-player puzzle format, SNAC, has also driven longer engagement, with sessions that include the format running approximately three times longer.

Rahul Humayan, partner at General Catalyst, said the platform was addressing demand for alternatives to conventional digital content.

"Negative content is consuming a growing share of our screen time, and Matiks is building the alternative: a social platform for brain games where people challenge friends, learn from one another and, soon, use AI to create games of their own. Sudhanshu, Sushant and Mohan have built one of the most engaged communities we have seen in consumer, from everyday players to world champions, and they are now taking it global. We are proud to partner with them as they make brain games a category of their own," he said.

Matiks will initially prioritise expansion in the US before entering other tier-one markets. It also plans to increase investments in engineering, AI, product, design, game development and growth, alongside scaling creator partnerships and global distribution.

The company plans to develop an AI-powered game creation engine that will allow users to create, publish and share brain games across multiple formats. It expects user-generated content to increase the variety of games available on the platform.
